html:
The shipping of indentured workers from India to sugar colonies in the Caribbean and South America, from 1838 to 1917. It was part of the wider system of Indian indenture that also sent workers to Mauritius, Natal and Fiji.

After the abolition of slavery and the end of "apprenticeship" in 1838, many freed people left the plantations. Planters looked for cheap labour. The first two ships reached British Guiana in 1838, and the first to Trinidad, the Fatel Razack, arrived in 1845.

Workers signed contracts, usually for five years, with a promise of passage home after ten. Most came from today's Bihar and Uttar Pradesh by way of Calcutta, with others from the south through Madras. Conditions were harsh and the pay low, and critics called it a new system of slavery. Indian nationalists campaigned against it until it ended in 1917.

Most stayed. Their descendants now form large parts of the population of Guyana, Trinidad and Suriname, where Divali, Phagwah, Indian food and chutney music are part of national life.
